questions.prompt: A particle moves along the $x$-axis in such a way that its position at time $t$ is given by $x(t)=3t^4-16t^3+24t^2$ for $-5\le t\le 5$.
questions.directions: Show the mathematical work supporting each answer.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Determine the velocity and acceleration of the particle at time $t$.
parts.solution: Differentiate the position function once to obtain velocity and twice to obtain acceleration.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: At what values of $t$ is the particle at rest?

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: At what values of $t$ does the particle change direction?
parts.solution: Because $v(t)=12t(t-2)^2$, the factor $(t-2)^2$ does not change sign at $t=2$. The velocity changes from negative to positive only at $t=0$.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: What is the velocity when the acceleration is first zero?
parts.solution: Solve $a(t)=12(3t-2)(t-2)=0$. The first zero in the interval is $t=\frac23$. Then $v\left(\frac23\right)=12\left(\frac23\right)\left(\frac23-2\right)^2=\frac{128}{9}$.

questions.facsimileAuthority: The source scan remains authoritative for historical wording; this record is a verified mathematical transcription.
questions.explanation: Velocity is the derivative of position and acceleration is the derivative of velocity. A particle changes direction only where velocity changes sign, not merely wherever velocity equals zero.
questions.workedSolution: Differentiate: $v(t)=x'(t)=12t^3-48t^2+48t=12t(t-2)^2$. Differentiate again: $a(t)=v'(t)=36t^2-96t+48=12(3t-2)(t-2)$. The particle is at rest at $t=0$ and $t=2$. Since $(t-2)^2\ge0$, the sign of $v$ is determined by the sign of $t$; hence the only direction change occurs at $t=0$. Acceleration is zero at $t=\frac23$ and $t=2$, so the first such time is $t=\frac23$. Substitution gives $v(\frac23)=\frac{128}{9}$.
questions.alternativeSolution: Use a sign chart for $v(t)=12t(t-2)^2$ to distinguish a zero of even multiplicity from a genuine sign change.
questions.noncalculatorSolution: All derivatives, factorizations, sign analysis, and substitutions can be completed exactly without a calculator.
questions.studentExplanation: The particle is at rest when $v=0$, but it changes direction only when the sign of $v$ changes. The double root at $t=2$ does not cause a sign change.
questions.teacherExplanation: Emphasize the distinction between rest and direction change. The even multiplicity of the velocity zero at $t=2$ is the central conceptual point.

commonMistakes: Listing both $t=0$ and $t=2$ as direction changes without checking the sign of velocity.
Using the zeros of acceleration to answer the rest question.
Selecting $t=2$ rather than the first chronological zero $t=\frac23$ in part (d).
Substituting into the position function instead of the velocity function in part (d).

classification.primaryTopic: Straight-line motion: position, velocity, acceleration, rest, and direction change
learningObjectives: Interpret velocity and acceleration as derivatives of position.
Determine when a particle is at rest.
Use the sign of velocity to identify changes in direction.

hints.text: Differentiate position to obtain velocity, then differentiate velocity to obtain acceleration.
A zero of velocity produces a direction change only if velocity changes sign there.

misconceptions: Every zero of velocity is automatically a direction change.
